tip: Auf Wiedersehen is the formal goodbye; with friends you would say Tschüss instead.
zu Mittag essen is literally to eat at midday, so German needs no separate word for lunch.
For no or not any before a noun, German uses kein, never nicht ein: kein Geld mehr.
du is the casual you, as in was machst du hier; with a stranger you would default to the formal Sie.
schulfrei is literally school-free; -frei attaches to a noun to mean without it, as in alkoholfrei or autofrei.
German has homesickness rather than being homesick: Heimweh haben, literally home-ache.
A modal verb brackets the sentence: Können opens it and the main verb haben comes at the very end.
In separable verbs the ge- of the participle sits inside: eingeschlafen is ein plus ge plus schlafen.
German has hunger rather than being hungry: Hunger haben is literally I have hunger.
With seit, German stays in the present: lerne seit einem Jahr is English have been learning for a year.
gern after a verb means like to: erzählt gern Geschichten is likes to tell stories.
German negates a noun with kein, not nicht: no more room becomes keinen Platz mehr.
seit with the present tense covers English has been doing: wartet schon seit einer Stunde is has been waiting an hour.
The verb stays second: after the fronted time phrase Um drei Uhr nachmittags, gibt comes right away.
vorlesen is separable: the vor breaks off to the very end, so liest and vor wrap the whole sentence.
für always takes the accusative, which is why it is für den gesamten Nahverkehr, den and not der.
Start with a time phrase and the verb still comes second, before the subject: Heute Nachmittag holt mein Vater, not mein Vater holt.
weil sends the verb to the end of its clause: weil der letzte Bus schon abgefahren ist, with ist last.
With no article, the adjective itself carries the case ending: mit frischem Brot, where -em marks the dative dem would have shown.
German yes/no questions need no do: Hast du Geschwister is literally Have you siblings, verb first.
Excited about is begeistert von in German, not über: begeistert von der neuen Ausstellung.
von always takes the dative, so eine becomes einer: träumst von einer Weltreise.
German uses the present with seit for ongoing time: wohnen seit fünf Jahren is English have been living five years.
fünf gerade sein lassen is literally to let five be an even number, meaning to accept small wrongness instead of correcting everything.
English not a single becomes kein, never nicht ein: kein einziges günstiges Hotelzimmer.
German has fear rather than being afraid: Angst haben vor, as in Angst vor Spinnen.
davon fuses da- with von, the preposition überzeugt takes, to mean of it or of that: fest davon überzeugt.
dass sends the verb to the end of its clause: dass das stimmt, with stimmt last.
German says allergic against, not to: allergisch gegen Nüsse und Erdbeeren.
The whole phrase Trotz des schlechten Wetters fills the first slot, so the verb comes next: gehen wir, not wir gehen.
With no article the adjective carries the case ending: kalten Kaffee shows the masculine accusative with -en.
Bare time expressions take the accusative, which turns jeder into jeden: jeden Morgen means every morning.
With no article the adjective shows gender and case itself: Frisches Brot takes the -es that das would otherwise carry.
fertig alone already means both finished and worn out; fix und fertig just intensifies it to completely wiped out.
den is accusative because of its job inside its own clause: meine Mutter backt den Kuchen.
Heft here means hilt or handle, not notebook: das Heft in der Hand is holding the handle, that is being in charge.
zwei linke Hände is literally two left hands, the German version of being all thumbs.
helfen takes a dative object, so in German you help to someone: er half seiner Nachbarin.
Without an article the adjective takes the ending itself: Heißer Tee carries the -er that der would otherwise show.
Separable verbs split in commands: zuhören becomes hör and then zu, with the prefix stranded at the end.
ein Brett vor dem Kopf is literally a board in front of your head, so you cannot see what is right there.
Here schon is a reassuring particle meaning you will manage alright, not its other sense already: wirst das schon schaffen.
noch nicht means not yet, literally still not: Ich bin noch nicht fertig.
A direct object turns der into den: den Garten is the thing being designed, so der Garten becomes den Garten.
Negate a noun with kein, not nicht: no idea becomes keine Ahnung, never nicht Ahnung.
kein takes the same endings as ein: keinen Grund shows the masculine accusative -en, just like einen Grund.
